title: Deep Data Lab
subtitle: The story above focused on the investigative path. This section exposes the underlying benchmark and diagnostic evidence for closer inspection.

holdout.label: Frozen Holdout
holdout.question: How did the routing approaches behave on the balanced frozen holdout?
holdout.caption: Descriptive comparison of semantic decision accuracy and operational request success across 50 frozen test cases. Infrastructure conditions, retry policies, gateway latency, and pricing models differed across systems; this does not establish a universal winner.
holdout.methodology: Provider comparisons were not normalized for latency, infrastructure, or cost accounting. Semantic accuracy reflects successful requests matching ground truth; all-attempt rate incorporates infrastructure drops.

progression.label: Experimental Progression
progression.question: How did the Jev evaluation program evolve across benchmark and diagnostic stages?
progression.figureTitle: Validation Suites (V1–V3) vs. Adaptive Diagnostic Probes (V4–V5)
progression.caption: Progression from initial formulation validation (V1–V3) to targeted adversarial stress testing (V4–V5). V4–V5 are adaptive diagnostic probe suites designed to find failure modes, not untouched holdouts.
progression.methodology: This trajectory is not a continuous model performance improvement curve. The evaluation objective shifted from stationary benchmark accuracy in V1–V3 to deliberate boundary search and cue-stripping in V4–V5.

boundary.label: Decision Boundary
boundary.question: Where did repeated routing behavior become mixed near semantic decision boundaries?
boundary.figureTitle: Repeated-Choice Distribution and Candidate Separation Across Boundary States
boundary.caption: Observed routing behavior across repeated identical evaluations of selected boundary states. Confidence represents candidate probability mass, margin represents top-two candidate separation, and choice proportions reflect empirical stochastic switching.
boundary.methodology: Repeated identical evaluations characterize empirical stochastic behavior under fixed prompts; they are not independent samples. Confidence is not calibrated correctness probability, and margin is candidate separation rather than a validated production threshold.
boundary.mobileScrollHint: Scroll horizontally to inspect all 5 boundary states →

explicitness.label: Implementation Explicitness
explicitness.question: How did the six discrete V8 state representations differ in recorded routing stability?
explicitness.figureTitle: Discrete State Variants C1–C6: Margin Separation and Instability Rates
explicitness.caption: Empirical comparison of six discrete prompt representations of missing implementation state. C1–C6 are distinct tested variants; this does not establish a continuous interpolation or a universal causal law across arbitrary agent prompts.
explicitness.methodology: C1 recorded mixed choices, while C2–C6 recorded a single SEARCH_CODE choice across their repeated evaluations. Candidate-separation signals also differed across these tested variants.

stability.label: Confidence & Stability
stability.question: Why must confidence, candidate margin, and repeated stability be treated as distinct signals?
stability.figureTitle: Conceptual Framework: Separating Probability Mass, Candidate Margin, and Empirical Frequency
stability.caption: Analytical guide to interpreting router uncertainty signals. High confidence can mask semantic edge-case errors, while low confidence can produce stable and correct decisions.
stability.methodology: Routing certainty signals should inform retry, clarification, or human-escalation policies, but should never be conflated with deterministic safety or permission enforcement.
